title: A2/A3 fixpipe byte quantization and FP16 dequantization straight from L0C to GM
surface: Tensor.requant(scale=, offset=) on an FP32 or INT32 L0C accumulator stored directly into a GM tensor of the destination dtype -- int8, uint8 and float16 -- with no UB staging; one kernel(mode="cube") launch per conversion on the shared A2/A3 vocabulary
study_for: The destination is GM and there is no UB anywhere. The fixpipe converts as it stores, so the conversion's rules -- rounding, the intermediate clamp, the offset, the final saturation -- all happen on the way out of L0C and cannot be inspected or repaired in between.

Byte quantization saturates twice and the order matters: scale, round to nearest even, clamp to the intermediate signed 9-bit range [-256, 255], add the offset, then saturate to the destination's own range. Adding the offset before the intermediate clamp, or skipping that clamp, gives a different answer -- at the planted boundary values, visibly so.

`qf_i8` and `qf_u8` are the *same kernel* with different destination dtypes: signedness follows the dtype. Keeping both is what turns that sentence into a check, because the unsigned path clamps to [0, 255] where the signed one clamps to [-128, 127] from the same intermediate value.

The scalar scale is truncated to the top 19 FP32 bits before it is applied, and the reference performs that truncation explicitly with a `0xFFFFE000` mask. At 0.5 and 0.25 the truncation is the identity -- `check_domain` asserts exactly that -- so it changes no value here while stating the rule that would matter for a scale where it did.

`check_domain` asserts exactly which clamps each dataset reaches, in both directions. Measured: the planted and random cases drive all three byte outputs to both ends, while the source case's products span only [-86, 82] and [-111, 94] and reach nothing but the unsigned floor. So the source case establishes the arithmetic and the rounding and nothing about the clamping -- worth knowing, because on its own it would pass every comparison while testing none of the saturation this conversion is mostly about.

Every output is compared as raw bytes, the FP16 one included: the reference builds its carriers with `struct.pack('<e', ...)` and an explicit overflow-to-infinity rule. Nothing is narrowed on the host, so a carrier is compared against a carrier and a rounding difference cannot be absorbed.
do_not_copy_when: Your operands are not integer-valued and bounded. The domain is finite FP16 integers in [-1024, 1024] and INT8 values; that is what makes the products exact and the byte comparison legitimate. Non-integral operands need their own reference for the rounding.
You are applying one saturation. There are two, in a fixed order, and a single clamp to the destination range agrees with this example only where the intermediate clamp never bites.
Your scale is not exact under the FP19 truncation. Then the truncation is part of the answer and needs its own reference; nothing here establishes how an arbitrary scale rounds.
You need the INT32-to-UINT8 path. The corrected sources have no unsigned entry for the integer accumulator, and this example does not claim one.
You are publishing through UB. This is the direct-GM path; the L0C-to-UB arrangement is a separate example with its own ownership handoff, and neither establishes the other.
